title: Tipiṭaka (the Pali Canon)
summary: The three 'baskets' of the Theravāda canon — Vinaya (monastic discipline), Sutta (discourses) and Abhidhamma (analysis of phenomena) — held to be the word of the Buddha as rehearsed at the First Council and transmitted orally until written down in Sri Lanka.

structure.description: Vinaya Piṭaka (Suttavibhaṅga, Khandhaka, Parivāra); Sutta Piṭaka (Dīgha, Majjhima, Saṃyutta, Aṅguttara and Khuddaka Nikāyas); Abhidhamma Piṭaka (seven books: Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, Paṭṭhāna)

tradition.text: rehearsed at the First Council at Rājagaha in the first rains after the parinibbāna (543 BCE by the Theravāda reckoning); written down on palm leaves at the Āloka-vihāra (Aluvihāra), Sri Lanka, under King Vaṭṭagāmaṇī Abhaya

scholarly.text: oral composition and redaction c. 5th–1st c. BCE; first written c. 29–17 BCE (Vaṭṭagāmaṇī); later KN books and the Abhidhamma the latest strata

editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

editions.licence: free distribution

editions.name: Pali Text Society romanized edition (1877 onward)
editions.licence: various

notes: The Fifth Council (Mandalay 1871, under King Mindon) inscribed the Tipiṭaka on 729 marble slabs at the Kuthodaw Pagoda; the Sixth Council (Yangon 1954–56) produced the Chaṭṭha Saṅgāyana text on which the Mahāsaṅgīti edition is based (recent events; recorded as metadata).

title: Vinaya Piṭaka
summary: The basket of discipline: the Pātimokkha rules for monks and nuns with their origin stories and analysis (Suttavibhaṅga), the procedures and customs of the Saṅgha — ordination, uposatha, rains retreat, robes, medicine, legal acts, the nuns' order and the first two councils (Khandhaka) — and a later manual (Parivāra).

structure.description: Suttavibhaṅga (Mahāvibhaṅga / Bhikkhuvibhaṅga and Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga); Khandhaka (Mahāvagga, 10 khandhakas; Cullavagga, 12 khandhakas); Parivāra

tradition.text: recited by Upāli at the First Council

scholarly.text: core rules and procedures c. 5th–4th c. BCE; narrative frame and Parivāra later (the Parivāra c. 1st c. BCE or later, compiled in Sri Lanka)

editions.name: Mahāsaṅgīti Tipiṭaka Buddhavasse 2500 (World Tipiṭaka edition, based on the Sixth Council text), as published by SuttaCentral in bilara-data (root/pli/ms); local copy in sources_raw/bilara-data
editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

title: Suttavibhaṅga
summary: The 'analysis of the rules': each Pātimokkha rule with the story of the incident that led the Buddha to lay it down, the rule itself, a word-commentary, the variations and the non-offence cases.

structure.description: Mahāvibhaṅga (the 227 bhikkhu rules) and Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga (the rules particular to nuns; of 311 bhikkhunī rules only those not shared with monks are analysed in full)

title: Mahāvibhaṅga (Bhikkhuvibhaṅga)
summary: The analysis of the 227 monks' rules in eight classes, beginning with the four pārājikas (sexual intercourse, theft, killing a human being, falsely claiming superhuman states).

structure.description: 4 pārājika, 13 saṅghādisesa, 2 aniyata, 30 nissaggiya pācittiya, 92 pācittiya, 4 pāṭidesanīya, 75 sekhiya, 7 adhikaraṇasamatha = 227

title: Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga
summary: The analysis of the nuns' rules, especially those not shared with monks (e.g. the four additional pārājikas).

structure.description: 311 rules: 8 pārājika, 17 saṅghādisesa, 30 nissaggiya pācittiya, 166 pācittiya, 8 pāṭidesanīya, 75 sekhiya, 7 adhikaraṇasamatha

title: Bhikkhu Pātimokkha
summary: The code of 227 rules recited by the monks' Saṅgha every fortnight on the uposatha day, with a confession of purity; called the 'heart' of the Vinaya.

structure.description: introduction (nidāna) + 4 pārājika, 13 saṅghādisesa, 2 aniyata, 30 nissaggiya pācittiya, 92 pācittiya, 4 pāṭidesanīya, 75 sekhiya, 7 adhikaraṇasamatha = 227 rules

editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

title: Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha
summary: The nuns' code of 311 rules recited fortnightly by the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha.

structure.description: 8 pārājika, 17 saṅghādisesa, 30 nissaggiya pācittiya, 166 pācittiya, 8 pāṭidesanīya, 75 sekhiya, 7 adhikaraṇasamatha = 311

title: Khandhaka
summary: The 'chapters' on Saṅgha procedure, framed by the story of the Buddha's awakening and the founding of the order (Mahāvagga 1) and closing with the first two councils (Cullavagga 11–12).

structure.description: 22 khandhakas: Mahāvagga 1–10, Cullavagga 1–12

title: Mahāvagga (Vinaya)
summary: Ten khandhakas: the Great Chapter (the awakening, the first sermon, the first disciples, ordination), uposatha, entering the rains, the invitation (pavāraṇā), leather, medicines, the kaṭhina, robes, Campā (validity of legal acts) and Kosambī (the quarrel at Kosambī).

structure.description: 1 Mahākhandhaka, 2 Uposatha, 3 Vassūpanāyika, 4 Pavāraṇā, 5 Camma, 6 Bhesajja, 7 Kaṭhina, 8 Cīvara, 9 Campeyya, 10 Kosambaka

editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

title: Cullavagga
summary: Twelve khandhakas: formal acts of the Saṅgha, probation, rehabilitation, settling disputes, minor matters, dwellings, schism (Devadatta), duties, suspending the Pātimokkha, the nuns (Mahāpajāpatī's ordination and the eight garudhammas), and the councils of the five hundred (Rājagaha) and the seven hundred (Vesālī).

structure.description: 1 Kamma, 2 Pārivāsika, 3 Samuccaya, 4 Samatha, 5 Khuddakavatthu, 6 Senāsana, 7 Saṅghabheda, 8 Vatta, 9 Pātimokkhaṭṭhapana, 10 Bhikkhunī, 11 Pañcasatika, 12 Sattasatika

editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

title: Parivāra
summary: A catechetical manual and summary of the Vinaya — lists, questions and answers on the rules and procedures — compiled later, traditionally ascribed to the elder Dīpa in Sri Lanka.

scholarly.text: later than the rest of the Vinaya, compiled in Sri Lanka (c. 1st c. BCE or later)

structure.description: about 19–21 sections (the count depends on the edition)

title: Sutta Piṭaka
summary: The basket of discourses: the Buddha's and his great disciples' teachings arranged in five collections (nikāya) by length (Dīgha, Majjhima), by topic (Saṃyutta), by number (Aṅguttara), and a miscellany (Khuddaka).

structure.description: Dīgha Nikāya (34 suttas), Majjhima Nikāya (152), Saṃyutta Nikāya (56 saṃyuttas), Aṅguttara Nikāya (11 nipātas), Khuddaka Nikāya (15 to 18 books by edition)

tradition.text: recited by Ānanda at the First Council

scholarly.text: c. 5th–3rd c. BCE for the core; some Khuddaka books to the 1st c. BCE or later

title: Dīgha Nikāya
summary: The 'long discourses': 34 suttas, including the Brahmajāla (62 views), Sāmaññaphala (the fruits of the contemplative life and the gradual training), Mahānidāna (dependent origination), Mahāparinibbāna (the last days), Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna, Aggañña (origins of society and caste) and Siṅgāla (lay ethics).

structure.description: 34 suttas in 3 vaggas: Sīlakkhandhavagga (DN 1–13), Mahāvagga (DN 14–23), Pāthikavagga (DN 24–34)

tradition.text: recited by Ānanda; entrusted to the pupils of Ānanda (commentarial account)

scholarly.text: c. 4th–3rd c. BCE for its redaction; many discourses older

editions.name: Mahāsaṅgīti Tipiṭaka Buddhavasse 2500 (World Tipiṭaka edition, based on the Sixth Council text), as published by SuttaCentral in bilara-data (root/pli/ms); local copy in sources_raw/bilara-data
editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

title: Majjhima Nikāya
summary: The 'middle-length discourses': 152 suttas on the whole range of the teaching — meditation (MN 10, 118, 119, 20), the Buddha's own quest (MN 26, 36), not-self and views (MN 22, 72, 63), kamma (MN 135–136), dependent origination (MN 38), the gradual training (MN 27, 39, 107), emptiness (MN 121–122) and dialogues with brahmins and Jains.

structure.description: 152 suttas in 3 paṇṇāsas (Mūla, Majjhima, Upari) of 5 vaggas each (the last paṇṇāsa has 52 suttas)

tradition.text: entrusted to the pupils of Sāriputta (commentarial account)

scholarly.text: c. 4th–3rd c. BCE for its redaction

editions.name: Mahāsaṅgīti Tipiṭaka Buddhavasse 2500 (World Tipiṭaka edition, based on the Sixth Council text), as published by SuttaCentral in bilara-data (root/pli/ms); local copy in sources_raw/bilara-data
editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

title: Saṃyutta Nikāya
summary: The 'connected discourses', grouped by topic into 56 saṃyuttas: verse dialogues with gods, Māra and brahmins (Sagāthāvagga), dependent origination (Nidānavagga), the aggregates (Khandhavagga), the six senses (Saḷāyatanavagga), and the path factors, awakening factors, satipaṭṭhāna, faculties, jhāna, ānāpānasati, stream-entry and the truths (Mahāvagga).

structure.description: 56 saṃyuttas in 5 vaggas: Sagātha (SN 1–11), Nidāna (12–21), Khandha (22–34), Saḷāyatana (35–44), Mahā (45–56); the commentarial count is 7,762 suttas, modern counts c. 2,900 because of abbreviation

tradition.text: entrusted to the pupils of Mahākassapa (commentarial account)

scholarly.text: c. 4th–3rd c. BCE; considered close in content to the Saṃyuktāgama (Sarvāstivāda)

editions.name: Mahāsaṅgīti Tipiṭaka Buddhavasse 2500 (World Tipiṭaka edition, based on the Sixth Council text), as published by SuttaCentral in bilara-data (root/pli/ms); local copy in sources_raw/bilara-data
editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

title: Aṅguttara Nikāya
summary: The 'numerical discourses', arranged in eleven books by the number of items treated (ones to elevens): the luminous mind (AN 1.51–52), the Kālāma teaching (AN 3.65), the four kinds of concentration development (AN 4.41), kamma as intention (AN 6.63), the eight worldly conditions, women's ordination (AN 8.51), the ten perceptions (AN 10.60), and much lay ethics.

structure.description: 11 nipātas (Ekaka to Ekādasaka); the commentarial count is 9,557 suttas, modern counts c. 8,000 (abbreviated repetitions)

tradition.text: entrusted to the pupils of Anuruddha (commentarial account)

scholarly.text: c. 4th–2nd c. BCE

editions.name: Mahāsaṅgīti Tipiṭaka Buddhavasse 2500 (World Tipiṭaka edition, based on the Sixth Council text), as published by SuttaCentral in bilara-data (root/pli/ms); local copy in sources_raw/bilara-data
editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

title: Khuddaka Nikāya
summary: The 'minor collection', a miscellany of verse and prose books ranging from the oldest strata (Aṭṭhaka and Pārāyana vaggas of the Sutta Nipāta, parts of the Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Thera- and Therīgāthā) to late works (Apadāna, Buddhavaṃsa, Cariyāpiṭaka, Niddesa, Paṭisambhidāmagga) and, in the Burmese canon, the Nettippakaraṇa, Peṭakopadesa and Milindapañha.

structure.description: Burmese (Sixth Council) canon: 18 books — Khuddakapāṭha, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Sutta Nipāta, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, Apadāna, Buddhavaṃsa, Cariyāpiṭaka, Jātaka, Niddesa (Mahā- and Cūḷa-), Paṭisambhidāmagga, Nettippakaraṇa, Peṭakopadesa, Milindapañha. Sri Lankan and Thai canons: the first 15 (without the last three).

scholarly.text: c. 5th c. BCE (oldest verse) to c. 1st c. CE (latest books)

notes: The count of books and the inclusion of Netti, Peṭakopadesa and Milindapañha differ between editions; the Thai edition has varied over time.

editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

title: Khuddakapāṭha
summary: A short handbook of nine texts for novices and recitation: the three refuges, the ten training rules, the 32 parts of the body, the novice's questions, the Maṅgala, Ratana and Mettā suttas, the Tirokuḍḍa (offering to the dead) and the Nidhikaṇḍa (the treasure of merit).

structure.description: 9 short texts (Saraṇattaya, Dasasikkhāpada, Dvattiṃsākāra, Kumārapañha, Maṅgala, Ratana, Tirokuḍḍa, Nidhikaṇḍa, Metta)

scholarly.text: compiled late (perhaps Sri Lanka), from older material

title: Dhammapada
summary: 423 verses in 26 chapters on the Dhamma as a way of life: mind as forerunner (1–2), hatred ceased by non-hatred (5), heedfulness, the mind, the fool and the wise, the arahant, the self, the world, the Buddha (183), happiness, craving, the path (277–279), the bhikkhu and the true brahmin.

structure.description: 26 vaggas, 423 verses

scholarly.text: c. 3rd c. BCE (compilation); parallels in the Gāndhārī Dharmapada, Patna Dharmapada and Udānavarga

editions.name: Mahāsaṅgīti Tipiṭaka Buddhavasse 2500 (World Tipiṭaka edition, based on the Sixth Council text), as published by SuttaCentral in bilara-data (root/pli/ms); local copy in sources_raw/bilara-data
editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

title: Udāna
summary: 80 short suttas in 8 vaggas, each culminating in an inspired utterance (udāna) of the Buddha: the awakening verses on dependent origination (1.1–3), the teaching to Bāhiya (1.10), Meghiya (4.1), the blind men and the elephant (6.4), and the four utterances on nibbāna (8.1–4).

structure.description: 8 vaggas of 10 suttas

scholarly.text: c. 4th–3rd c. BCE

editions.name: Mahāsaṅgīti Tipiṭaka Buddhavasse 2500 (World Tipiṭaka edition, based on the Sixth Council text), as published by SuttaCentral in bilara-data (root/pli/ms); local copy in sources_raw/bilara-data
editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

title: Itivuttaka
summary: 112 short suttas 'thus it was said', prose followed by verse, arranged by number (ones to fours); by tradition remembered by the laywoman Khujjuttarā, who repeated the Buddha's words to Queen Sāmāvatī's household.

structure.description: 112 suttas in 4 nipātas

tradition.text: heard and repeated by Khujjuttarā (commentarial account)

scholarly.text: c. 4th–3rd c. BCE

title: Sutta Nipāta
summary: A collection of 71 (72 by some counts) verse suttas in five vaggas — Uraga, Cūḷa, Mahā, Aṭṭhaka, Pārāyana — including the Mettā, Ratana and Maṅgala suttas, the Padhāna (the bodhisatta's struggle with Māra), the Vāseṭṭha (true brahmin), and the Aṭṭhakavagga and Pārāyanavagga, counted among the oldest Buddhist poetry.

structure.description: 5 vaggas: Uraga (12), Cūḷa (14), Mahā (12), Aṭṭhaka (16), Pārāyana (intro + 16 questions + epilogue)

scholarly.text: Aṭṭhaka- and Pārāyanavagga among the oldest strata (commented on in the canonical Niddesa); the collection as a whole later

editions.name: Mahāsaṅgīti Tipiṭaka Buddhavasse 2500 (World Tipiṭaka edition, based on the Sixth Council text), as published by SuttaCentral in bilara-data (root/pli/ms); local copy in sources_raw/bilara-data
editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

title: Aṭṭhakavagga
summary: The fourth vagga of the Sutta Nipāta (16 poems): the sage (muni) who clings to no view, does not dispute, is free of sensual desire and of 'mine', and does not take a stand on purity by views, rules or vows.

scholarly.text: among the oldest Buddhist texts; a Chinese parallel (Arthapada, T 198) exists

title: Pārāyanavagga
summary: The fifth vagga of the Sutta Nipāta: sixteen brahmin students of Bāvarī question the Buddha on crossing the flood, on the end of craving and on nibbāna ('the way to the far shore').
location_in_parent: Snp 5.1–5.18 (SuttaCentral numbering: 5.1 the introductory verses, 5.2–5.17 the sixteen questions, 5.18 the epilogue)

scholarly.text: among the oldest Buddhist texts; commented on in the Cūḷaniddesa

title: Vimānavatthu
summary: Stories of the heavenly mansions (vimāna): deities tell Moggallāna and others what meritorious deed — often a small gift or act of faith — led to their celestial rebirth.

structure.description: 85 stories in 7 vaggas (by one count)

scholarly.text: late canonical (c. 3rd–1st c. BCE)

title: Petavatthu
summary: Stories of the hungry ghosts (peta): beings suffering the results of miserliness and wrongdoing, and the transfer of merit (dakkhiṇā) by relatives that relieves them.

structure.description: 51 stories in 4 vaggas (by one count)

scholarly.text: late canonical (c. 3rd–1st c. BCE)

title: Theragāthā
summary: The verses of the elder monks: some 1,279 verses attributed to 264 arahant monks describing their going forth, struggle and liberation (e.g. Aṅgulimāla, Thag 16.8; Mahākassapa, Thag 18.1).

structure.description: 21 nipātas (by number of verses per poem)

scholarly.text: compiled over several centuries (c. 5th–3rd c. BCE)

editions.name: Mahāsaṅgīti Tipiṭaka Buddhavasse 2500 (World Tipiṭaka edition, based on the Sixth Council text), as published by SuttaCentral in bilara-data (root/pli/ms); local copy in sources_raw/bilara-data
editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

title: Therīgāthā
summary: The verses of the elder nuns: 73 poems (522–524 verses) by or about arahant nuns — Paṭācārā, Kisāgotamī, Khemā, Uppalavaṇṇā, Mahāpajāpatī, Ambapālī, Sumedhā — on grief, renunciation, meditation and release; the earliest collection of women's religious poetry in India.

structure.description: 16 nipātas, 73 poems

scholarly.text: compiled c. 5th–3rd c. BCE

editions.name: Mahāsaṅgīti Tipiṭaka Buddhavasse 2500 (World Tipiṭaka edition, based on the Sixth Council text), as published by SuttaCentral in bilara-data (root/pli/ms); local copy in sources_raw/bilara-data
editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

title: Apadāna
summary: Legends of the past lives of monk and nun arahants (Thera- and Therī-apadāna) and of the Buddha, showing the meritorious deeds under former Buddhas that bore fruit in their liberation.

structure.description: Buddhāpadāna, Paccekabuddhāpadāna, Therāpadāna (c. 550), Therī-apadāna (40)

scholarly.text: among the latest canonical books (c. 2nd–1st c. BCE)

title: Buddhavaṃsa
summary: The chronicle of the Buddhas: the ascetic Sumedha's vow at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara to become a Buddha, and the lives of the twenty-four Buddhas who followed up to Gotama.

structure.description: 28 chapters (the 25 Buddhas from Dīpaṅkara to Gotama, plus the jewel-walk, the other Buddhas and the distribution of relics)

scholarly.text: late canonical (c. 2nd–1st c. BCE)

title: Cariyāpiṭaka
summary: 35 verse accounts of the Buddha's former lives illustrating the fulfilment of the perfections (pāramī) — giving, virtue, renunciation, determination, truthfulness, loving-kindness and equanimity.

structure.description: 3 vaggas, 35 stories (only seven of the ten perfections are illustrated)

scholarly.text: late canonical (c. 1st c. BCE)

title: Jātaka
summary: The canonical verses of 547 stories of the bodhisatta's former births; the prose stories that frame them belong to the commentary (Jātakaṭṭhakathā), which also contains the Nidānakathā biography of the Buddha.

structure.description: 547 jātakas in 22 nipātas by number of verses; the last ten (Mahānipāta) include the Vessantara Jātaka

scholarly.text: verse core c. 3rd c. BCE onward; prose commentary 5th c. CE

title: Mahāniddesa
summary: A canonical word-commentary on the Aṭṭhakavagga of the Sutta Nipāta, ascribed to Sāriputta.

scholarly.text: c. 2nd–1st c. BCE

title: Cūḷaniddesa
summary: A canonical word-commentary on the Pārāyanavagga and the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta, ascribed to Sāriputta.

scholarly.text: c. 2nd–1st c. BCE

title: Paṭisambhidāmagga
summary: The 'path of discrimination', an Abhidhamma-style treatise in the Sutta Piṭaka ascribed to Sāriputta: 73 kinds of knowledge, ānāpānasati, the faculties, emptiness, the kinds of liberation and the 'path of discrimination'.

structure.description: 3 vaggas (Mahā, Yuganaddha, Paññā), 30 kathās

scholarly.text: c. 2nd c. BCE

notes: Treated in depth by U37 with the Visuddhimagga, which draws on it.

title: Nettippakaraṇa
summary: A hermeneutical guide ('the guide') for explaining the suttas, by sixteen modes of conveying (hāra), five methods (naya) and eighteen root terms; ascribed to Mahākaccāna. Canonical only in the Burmese Khuddaka Nikāya.

tradition.text: taught by Mahākaccāna and approved by the Buddha

scholarly.text: c. 1st c. BCE – 1st c. CE

title: Peṭakopadesa
summary: An older, related hermeneutical treatise on the method of interpreting the teaching (the four truths as the frame), ascribed to Mahākaccāna; canonical in the Burmese Khuddaka Nikāya.

scholarly.text: c. 1st c. BCE – 1st c. CE

title: Milindapañha
summary: The Questions of King Milinda: the Indo-Greek king Menander questions the monk Nāgasena on not-self (the chariot), rebirth without transmigration (the flame), kamma, nibbāna and apparent inconsistencies in the texts (dilemmas). Canonical in the Burmese Khuddaka Nikāya.

structure.description: 7 books; books 1–3 the older core, 4–7 (dilemmas, similes) later additions

tradition.text: the dialogue of Nāgasena and King Milinda (Menander I, r. c. 165/155–130 BCE)

scholarly.text: core c. 1st c. BCE – 1st c. CE, expanded later; a Chinese parallel (Nāgasena Bhikṣu Sūtra) has only the core

title: Māra Saṃyutta
summary: Twenty-five encounters in which Māra tries to frighten, tempt or confuse the Buddha and is recognised and defeated ('I know you, Evil One').

editions.name: Mahāsaṅgīti Tipiṭaka Buddhavasse 2500 (World Tipiṭaka edition, based on the Sixth Council text), as published by SuttaCentral in bilara-data (root/pli/ms); local copy in sources_raw/bilara-data
editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

title: Bhikkhunī Saṃyutta
summary: Ten verse dialogues in which Māra challenges nuns (Āḷavikā, Somā, Kisāgotamī, Vijayā, Uppalavaṇṇā, Cālā, Upacālā, Sīsupacālā, Selā, Vajirā), and each refutes him — including Somā on women's capacity for wisdom and Vajirā on the 'being' as a convention like 'chariot'.

editions.name: Mahāsaṅgīti Tipiṭaka Buddhavasse 2500 (World Tipiṭaka edition, based on the Sixth Council text), as published by SuttaCentral in bilara-data (root/pli/ms); local copy in sources_raw/bilara-data
editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral
